newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria risks Ogoni-type crisis in tribal feud.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria risks Ogoni-type crisis in tribal feud.

text.p: Ethnic clashes sweeping Nigeria's oil-producing Delta state in the midwest could degenerate into a worse crisis than the one that engulfed Ogoniland in the southeast, according to Nigerian analysts.
The military government last Tuesday sent troops to Warri city to try to curb month-long carnage unleashed by militant youths protesting over the relocation of their municipal headquarters.
A navy ship sent a week ago to clear waterways blocked by the fighters has yet to move in because of the shallow Escravos River it has to navigate, according to newspaper reports.

"The Warri crisis is akin to the Ogoni issue and potentially can cause far more damage for Nigeria than Ogoni has done," said Oscar Ede, a former researcher at the Nigerian Institute of International Affairs in Lagos who lives in Warri.

Three tribes, the Ijaw, Itsekiri and Urhobo, inhabit Warri and like those in other oil-producing areas, have long been restive over the perception that the oil wealth derived from their land ends up in the pockets of a few elite.

Oil output in Ogoni, although small, has ceased since 1993 when youths rioted to back demands for a fairer share of oil revenues, self-determination for the tribe and compensation for ecological damage from oil activities.
The Ogoni crisis erupted in murders which led to the hanging in 1995 of nine Ogoni minority rights activists including author Ken Saro-Wiwa, provoking worldwide condemnation.

"While the Ogonis were protesting, the Ijaws, from whose land the bulk of the oil produced in Nigeria onshore is derived, were quietly arming themselves and that is why the fighting in Warri has been so bloody," said Ede.

Scores of people are reported to have died in the fighting in Warri, triggered when the headquarters of Warri south local government council was moved by the government from Ogbe-ijoh, an Ijaw town, to Ogidigben in Itsekiri area.
Homes of prominent people in the area have been burned and reports of kidnappings have been rife.

Oil production, Nigeria's economic backbone, is threatened and oil giant Shell company, the biggest operator in Nigeria, has reduced output in the area by 20 percent, pulled out some staff and delayed exports.
To many people such as Richard Tosanwumi, a former Delta state commissioner who lives in Warri, the relocation of the council headquarters was only the immediate cause of the clashes.
"The crisis in Warri is deep-rooted and multi-dimensional," he wrote in the independent Guardian newspaper last Thursday.
The three tribes there have long been at loggerheads over who should control the affairs of the second most important oil city in Nigeria.
The Ijaws are Nigeria's fourth largest tribe but because they are spread among six states, they are in the minority everywhere except in the newly created Bayelsa state.
Ijaws in Warri considered the relocation of the Warri south council capital further evidence of their marginalisation.
"If the federal government wants this thing to end today they can do it. Give us back our local government. That is the simple truth," said Fedudu Zimughan, an Ijaw lawyer in Warri.
But state officials say while the solution to the immediate crisis appears simple, no government worth its salt will succumb to brute force.
"If government bows to the pressure of violence it will be sending a wrong signal nationwide," said a federal official.
Similar protests have taken place in other parts of Nigeria since the local council restructuring in March. Warri got prominence because of the viciousness and the threat to oil.
Yet if not checked soon, there is a risk of the skirmishes spreading to other areas inhabited by the Ijaws, in sympathy with their kin in Warri, with serious consequences for overall oil production.

"The possibility of the crisis spreading to other Ijaw areas is real," said Ede. "Should that happen, it will not be possible for government to isolate it as it has done in Ogoni because while the Ogonis are only 500,000, the Ijaws taken together are more than five million," he added.
